name: Dunes
notes: Coastal and inland sand dunes: sand-binding rhizomatous grasses on mobile foredunes, sedges and creeping herbs behind, and scattered pine/juniper/willow scrub on stabilised grey dunes. Drawn on Atlantic and Baltic Europe, eastern and Pacific North America, and Australian foredunes.

canopy.name: Scots pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 5-7 cotyledons; in its first year it has single, flat, finely serrated primary needles 2-3 cm long, then short, twisted, blue-green paired needles. Young trees are regular, bushy cones; later the lower branches drop and the crown becomes flat or rounded above a tall trunk whose upper bark is orange and flaky.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 35 m, over 45 m on the best sites; normally lives 150-300 years, over 760 in Lapland; first-year seedlings have single serrated leaves 2-3 cm; seeds released 22-24 months after pollination); growth and first cones from European yield tables

canopy.source: Eurasia, Scotland to Siberia; 20–35 m. Orange upper bark; the boreal and heath pine. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the acorn sprouts soon after falling, and seedlings can grow 1.2 m in the first year. Young shoots and sprouts often have larger leaves with a few sharp, holly-like teeth, while adult leaves are small, entire and rolled under. Saplings are slender whips; root and collar sprouts make thickets, and later the crown spreads wide and low.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (flowers Mar-May; acorns ripen in Sep of the first year and fall before Dec; annual crops; 776 sound acorns/kg; intermediate shade tolerance; open-grown trunks to 200 cm dbh, crowns to 46 m); USDA FEIS (seedlings can grow 1.2 m in the first year; sprouts 0.3 m tall can bear acorns); lifespan estimated

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics and FEIS Quercus virginiana (pollen shed in the first 2 weeks of April; acorns long, tapered, dark brown to black, mature in Sep of the first year and fall before Dec; crops annual, often abundant; 776 sound acorns/kg); NC State Extension (acorns 1.9-2.5 cm on long stalks, Sep-Nov); per-tree crop estimated

canopy.name: Sand pine
canopy.origin: Florida and the Alabama Gulf coast

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with a whorl of cotyledons and single blue-green primary needles, then soft paired needles 5-9 cm. Saplings grow fast into bushy, narrow cones, branched to the ground; they keep their dead lower limbs, and by 30-40 years they are crooked, often forked, flat-topped little trees.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 1 (Brendemuehl, Pinus clausa): cones from about age 5; Ocala variety serotinous, Choctawhatchee variety opens its cones at maturity; very intolerant; stands break up after 50-70 years

canopy.source: Pinus clausa, sand pine: deep white sands of Florida and the Alabama coast, the Choctawhatchee variety on old coastal dunes of the Gulf; small crooked pine 5-21 m with paired needles 5-9 cm, keeping its dead lower limbs — USDA Silvics of North America vol. 1 (Brendemuehl); Kew POWO; Gymnosperm Database.

canopy.name: Pitch pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-8 cotyledons and single primary needles, then stiff yellow-green needles in threes. Seedlings bend over and root at the crook, and a young plant cut or burned to the ground sprouts again from buds at its root collar; saplings are open, irregular cones that already carry small cones at 3-4 years.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 1 (Little & Garrett, Pinus rigida): cones as early as age 3; sprouts from the root collar and dormant trunk buds after fire or cutting; few live past 200 years, the oldest about 450

canopy.source: Pinus rigida, pitch pine: dry sands of the Atlantic coastal plain, the dunes and pine barrens of Cape Cod, Long Island and New Jersey, inland to the Appalachians; 6-25 m (stunted on dunes), stiff needles in threes 7-13 cm and tufts of needles sprouting straight from the trunk — USDA Silvics of North America vol. 1; Kew POWO.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with small oval cotyledons, then narrow, aromatic, olive-green leaves toothed near the tip and dotted with tiny amber resin glands, as in the adult. It soon branches from the base into a dense, twiggy evergreen bush; nitrogen-fixing root nodules let it grow fast (often ~1 m a year) on poor sand, and it spreads by root sprouts into thickets.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 14 m; dioecious catkins late winter-spring; waxy globular fruit in late summer-fall; birds strip the wax, needed for germination); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Myrica (small waxy dry drupes persisting over winter; no endosperm); growth and ages estimated

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (dioecious, wind-pollinated catkins late winter-spring; fruit ripe late summer-fall, globular with a pale blue-grey wax coat, used for bayberry candles); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Myrica (tiny dry waxy drupes that persist on the shrub over winter); set and crop estimated

shrub.name: Beach plum

growth.juvenile_note: The stone needs a winter of cold, moist sand before it sprouts. The seedling is a slender reddish twig with small, finely toothed, downy oval leaves. It branches low and suckers from the roots, so in a few years it is a low, dense, twiggy dune thicket that is white with blossom before the leaves.
growth.source: Uva 2003 HortTechnology (beach plum: cold-moist stratification of the stones, fruiting from about the third year, suckering); USDA NRCS Plant Guide; lifespan estimated

shrub.source: Prunus maritima, beach plum: coastal dunes and sandy shores from New Brunswick and Maine to Maryland, low suckering shrub 1-2 m (to 3 m) with finely toothed, downy-backed leaves, white flowers before the leaves and purple plums with a waxy bloom — Kew POWO; USDA NRCS Plant Guide; Uva 2003 HortTechnology 13: 388-391.

bark.notes: dark grey-brown, smooth with pale horizontal lenticels, like a small cherry

leaf.notes: dull green, finely and sharply toothed, softly downy beneath

flower.form: white five-petalled flowers 1-1.5 cm in clusters of 2-3, before the leaves

fruit.form: round plums 1.2-2.5 cm, purple to blue-black with a waxy bloom

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; white blossom in May, red-orange leaves in autumn

shrub.name: Sand cherry
shrub.origin: Great Lakes and NE North America

growth.juvenile_note: After a winter's cold stratification the stone sends up a thin red-brown shoot with narrow leaves, toothed toward the tip and pale beneath. Buried by blowing sand it roots along its stems and sends up new shoots, so a young plant becomes a loose, sprawling clump of wiry stems on the open dune.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Prunus: cold stratification 90-150 days); Flora of North America vol. 9 (P. pumila on dunes and sandy shores); first fruiting and lifespan estimated

shrub.source: Prunus pumila, sand cherry: open dunes, beaches and sandy shores of the Great Lakes (var. pumila) and sandy or rocky ground of northeastern North America; sprawling to upright shrub 0.3-2 m, narrow leaves toothed toward the tip and pale beneath, white flowers and small purple-black cherries — Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 9 (Rosaceae).

growth.juvenile_note: The seedling is one upright stem with narrow, grey-green, rosemary-like leaves in whorls of four, felted white underneath with rolled-under edges. It branches freely from low down, so by its second year it is already a dense, rounded, grey-green bun of stiff leafy stems that flowers while still small.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Westringia fruticosa): coastal New South Wales shrub with white, hairy, two-lipped flowers spotted orange to purple, flowering all year. Size and fast growth from horticultural descriptions; germination (usually grown from cuttings), first flowering and lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (Westringia fruticosa, Westringia): white hairy flowers with a two-lobed upper lip and orange-to-purple spots, two fertile stamens, flowering all year. Flower size, fruit (four tiny nutlets held in the calyx), pollinators, timings and crop estimated from the genus and the mint family.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two cotyledons, then feathery bipinnate juvenile leaves (like a tiny fern frond) for the first season or two, gradually replaced by long, flat, bright-green phyllodes with 2-4 parallel veins. Young plants are fast, bushy, many-branched shrubs that flower by year 2-3. Mass germination follows fire.
growth.source: Herbiguide (feathery juvenile leaves for the first season or two; prolific seed at 2-3 yr; lives ~50 yr in native range, often <25 yr elsewhere; seedlings in winter and after fire); IUCN GISD (sexual maturity 2-3 yr; up to 11,500 seeds/tree; seeds viable ~50 yr)

fruiting.source: Herbiguide (golden cylindrical spikes 20-50 mm, usually paired in leaf axils, Jun-Oct; pods 50-150 mm, straight or curled, 4-10 seeds); IUCN GISD (flowers Jul-Aug native, Feb-Mar in Portugal with pods formed Mar-Jul; up to 11,500 seeds per tree)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are stiff, broad, blue-grey grass tufts on bare sand. They send out long rhizomes that throw up new tufts and grow up through burial by blowing sand, building low dunes of coarse, glaucous blue leaves topped by thick, wheat-like flower spikes up to about 1.5 m.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Leymus arenarius: dune-building grass, notably in Iceland after volcanic events; salt-tolerant germination; nitrogen boosts growth and seed yield; mycorrhizae aid seedling survival); growth and ages estimated from dune-grass ecology.

ground.name: Marram grass
ground.source: Ammophila arenaria, European Atlantic/Mediterranean foredunes (A. breviligulata in NE America), the archetypal sand-binder, 0.6-1.2 m — Wikipedia

traits.leaf_shape: narrow grass blades in a dense tussock
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.note: tightly inrolled grey-green leaves; tillers from deep rhizomes

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are rare (low seed viability and survival): a thin bright green blade in a damp dune slack, becoming a small tuft of in-rolled, sharp-tipped grey-green leaves. Most new plants grow from buried rhizome pieces. Tufts climb up through accreting sand, lengthening their leaves when buried, and become stiff, dense, spiky clumps of wiry rolled leaves up to 1.2 m.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Ammophila arenaria: stems to 1.2 m; rhizomes grow 2 m sideways in 6 months; one clump makes ~100 new shoots a year; seeds ripen by September and germinate the next spring, low viability and seedling survival; flowers May-Aug, panicle to 30 cm; survives burial >1 yr). Clump growth, first flowering and lifespan estimated.

ground.name: Bee orchid

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-like seed germinates only with a Tulasnella fungus, forming a tiny underground protocorm fed by the fungus for months to years. The first visible plant is a small rosette of 2-5 grey-green, oval-lance leaves that appears in autumn and grows slowly through winter; after several years a 20-40 cm stem rises in early summer with up to 12 flowers whose furry brown lip mimics a bee.
growth.source: Wikipedia Ophrys apifera (rosettes appear in autumn and grow through winter; flowers mid-April in S Europe, June-July in UK; 1-12 flowers; mostly self-pollinating in the north, Eucera bees in the Mediterranean; germination needs Tulasnella and may take months or years underground); Wells & Cox population studies (short-lived, often flowers once or twice)

repro.note: dust seed by wind; germinates only where its fungus lives (reads mycorrhizal presence); most species need one specific pollinator

ground.source: Mediterranean and W European grassland on lime. Mimics a bee; on chalk and limestone. Kew POWO.

ground.name: Bracken

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants appear 6-7 weeks after spores land on burnt or disturbed bare soil: the first fronds are small, simple and lobed, becoming finely divided and adult-like after about 18 weeks. After up to 10 fronds a rhizome starts, which may grow 2 m in the first year; by year two the patch can be about 2 m across, sending up single, triangular, much-divided fronds from underground.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pteridium aquilinum (young plants 6-7 weeks after spores shed; adult-like fronds after 18 weeks; rhizome to 217 cm in year 1; spores usually in the 3rd-4th season; cover under 5% below 25% of full sun); Wikipedia (individual rhizomes live up to 72 yr; colonies 650 to over 1,400 yr old).

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Every continent but Antarctica; dry hillsides, heath, burns — the first thing back after fire; toxic to browsers. Kew POWO.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are uncommon (only 21-48% of florets set seed); most plants start as a rhizome piece or a planted culm that sends up a tuft of stiff, rolled, grey-green blades and 35-40 new culms in its first season. Rhizomes run 1-3.5 m a year under the sand, lining up new tufts; tufts thicken under burial and from year 2 send up tight, spike-like, straw-coloured panicles.
growth.source: USDA NRCS plant guide (Ammophila breviligulata): >90% germination after cold stratification; 21-48% of florets set viable seed; one culm yields ~35-40 culms per season; rhizomes spread 1.2-3.5 m/yr, over 12 m from the parent; 0.3-1.5 m tall; tolerates ~30 cm of sand a year; seed heads late Jul-Aug. First seed and lifespan (decline on stable sand) estimated.

ground.name: Sand-hill screw-moss
ground.origin: Europe and North Africa, coastal dunes

growth.juvenile_note: New patches start from spores or broken shoots lodged in loose sand: a green protonemal film, then tiny upright shoots. They grow up through sand as it is buried, 1-4 cm tall, forming loose golden-green carpets; each shoot is a star of recurved, hair-pointed leaves when wet and a tight silvery twist when dry.
growth.source: Atherton, Bosanquet & Lawley 2010 Mosses and Liverworts of Britain and Ireland: a field guide (Syntrichia ruraliformis: yellowish-green patches on mobile and semi-fixed dunes, leaves recurved when moist with long hyaline hair-points, twisted when dry); establishment, growth and age estimated

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Syntrichia ruraliformis (syn. Tortula ruraliformis), sand-hill screw-moss: the moss of mobile and grey dunes in Atlantic and Baltic Europe, binding the sand between marram tufts; shoots 1-4 cm in loose golden-green carpets, leaves with long silvery hair-points, twisting when dry — Atherton et al. 2010 (British Bryological Society field guide); EU habitat 2130.

leaf.notes: golden-green stars of recurved leaves with silvery hair-points when wet; tight silvery-brown twists when dry

appearance.silhouette: golden-green moss carpets between marram tufts
appearance.refs: Atherton et al. 2010; British Bryological Society

ground.name: Dune cup lichen
ground.origin: Europe and North Africa, grey dunes

growth.juvenile_note: Starts from a scrap of squamule blown or kicked onto open, stable dune sand: a few tiny yellow-green scales. They lengthen into narrow, forked, strap-like squamules up to 1.5 cm that curl inward when dry to show white undersides, slowly knitting into loose pale carpets between the grasses.
growth.source: Smith et al. 2009 The Lichens of Great Britain and Ireland (Cladonia foliacea: squamules to 1.5 cm, yellow-green above, white below, inrolled when dry; on dunes and dry sandy or calcareous grassland); growth and ages estimated

repro.note: spores (which must meet their alga again) and, far more often, thallus fragments broken off and carried by wind, water and trampling; no flowers; grows only while wet

ground.source: Cladonia foliacea: lichen of grey (fixed) dunes and dry open sandy and calcareous grassland in Europe and North Africa; narrow forked squamules to 1.5 cm, yellow-green above and white below, curling up when dry into pale carpets; a character species of grey dunes — Smith et al. 2009 The Lichens of Great Britain and Ireland; EU Habitats Directive 2130.

leaf.notes: narrow forked strap-like scales, yellow-green above and white below, curling inward when dry

appearance.seasonal: white and curled when dry, greener and flatter when wet
appearance.silhouette: pale yellow-white curled carpets on grey-dune sand

ground.name: Heath reindeer lichen

growth.juvenile_note: A new patch starts from a broken fragment lodged in open heath or dune sand: a few pale, hollow, branching stalks a centimetre tall. Growing a few millimetres a year at the tips and dying at the base, they build dense, springy, pale grey-yellow cushions 3-8 cm deep, branching mostly in threes, the tips pointing every way.
growth.source: Smith et al. 2009 The Lichens of Great Britain and Ireland (Cladonia portentosa: dense cushions to 8 cm, branching mostly in threes, tips not turned one way; dune heath and lowland heath); growth rate taken from reindeer lichens, ages estimated

repro.note: spores (which must meet their alga again) and, far more often, thallus fragments broken off and carried by wind, water and trampling; no flowers; grows only while wet

ground.source: Cladonia portentosa: the reindeer lichen of Atlantic lowland and dune heaths of Europe and coastal north-eastern (and, subsp. pacifica, north-western) North America; pale grey-yellow cushions 3-8 cm of hollow stalks branching mostly in threes, tips spreading every way (unlike C. rangiferina) — Smith et al. 2009; Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff 2001 Lichens of North America.

leaf.notes: pale grey-yellow, densely branched hollow stalks in springy cushions, tips spreading every way

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; crisp and paler when dry

growth.source: Smith et al. 2009 The Lichens of Great Britain and Ireland (Cetraria aculeata, syn. Cornicularia aculeata: shrubby, dark brown, spiny-branched tufts to 5 cm on sandy heaths and dunes); growth and ages estimated

leaf.notes: stiff, round, shiny dark brown to blackish branches bristling with tiny spines

appearance.seasonal: dark and crisp when dry, olive-brown when wet

ground.name: Dune stinkhorn
ground.origin: Europe and North America, sandy ground

repro.note: The mycelium lives in the dune sand on buried plant debris; the fruiting body hatches from a pinkish-violet egg in hours and lasts a day or two. Flies carry the spores away in the slime; 'wind' stands in for the flies, 'rhizome' for the mycelium in the sand.

ground.source: Phallus hadriani, dune stinkhorn: saprotroph of coastal sand dunes and sandy soils in Europe and North America; hatches from a pinkish-violet egg 3-6 cm into a white spongy stem 10-20 cm with an olive-brown slime-covered honeycombed head — Pegler, Laessoe & Spooner 1995 British Puffballs, Earthstars and Stinkhorns; Index Fungorum.

cap.form: conical honeycombed head 3-5 cm under olive-brown spore slime, on a tall white spongy stem rising from a pinkish-violet egg
